The Work, Torah Thought and Legacy of Rabbi Yosef ibn Lev (the Maharival): A Pillar of Halakhic Instruction from the Ottoman Empire
Introduction and Historical Context: The Halakhic Renaissance of the Exiles from Spain in the Ottoman Empire
The 16th century was marked by an immense historical and spiritual transformation in the history of the Jewish people [cite: 1, 2]. The Expulsion from Spain (1492) and the decrees in Portugal (1497) uprooted hundreds of thousands of Jews from their homes, and they sought refuge throughout the Mediterranean basin [cite: 1, 2, 3]. The Ottoman Empire, under the rule of the sultans Bayezid II and Suleiman the Magnificent, opened its gates to the exiles and granted them religious freedom and opportunities for economic development [cite: 1, 2]. In the large urban centers, and in particular in Salonika and Constantinople (Istanbul), vibrant Jewish concentrations arose which within a short time became the leading centers of Torah and halakhic ruling in the Jewish world [cite: 1, 2, 3].
In this period, which was defined in retrospect as the decisive transitional generation between the period of the Rishonim and the period of the Acharonim, the sages of the generation were required to cope with unprecedented communal, moral and halakhic challenges [cite: 1, 2, 4]. The questions on the agenda encompassed the rehabilitation of the communities, the settling of the personal status of tens of thousands of Conversos (anusim), the solution of the problems of agunot, the organization of the laws of taxation and trade, and the reformulation of the literature of halakhic ruling [cite: 1, 2, 3]. Within this fabric of giants, which included figures such as Rabbi Yosef Karo, Rabbi Yosef Taitazak and Rabbi Shmuel de Medina (the Maharashdam), the figure of Rabbi Yosef ben David ibn Lev, known by his Torah appellation Maharival, stood out [cite: 3, 4, 5, 6]. The Maharival cast a unique mold of deep scholarship, Talmudic sharpness and resolute halakhic ruling, displaying public courage and a willingness to pay a heavy personal price for the halakhic and moral principles in which he believed [cite: 3, 7, 8].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Life, the Vicissitudes of His Fate and His Public Struggles
His Youth and His Service in Monastir
Rabbi Yosef ben David ibn Lev was born between the years 5260 and 5265 (approximately 1503–1505) in the city of Monastir (today Bitola in North Macedonia), which was then under the rule of the Ottoman Empire [cite: 3, 4, 7]. He grew up in a distinguished Torah home; his father, Rabbi David ibn Lev, was among the notables of the community and its sages [cite: 3, 4]. He acquired his Torah mainly from a relative of his, the Gaon Rabbi Yitzchak ibn Tzaddik ibn Lev, who served as his foremost teacher and set his path in the study of Torah [cite: 3, 4]. Already in his youth he revealed himself as an exceptional prodigy, with comprehensive mastery of the Shas and the halakhic authorities, and he was appointed to serve as rabbi, judge and halakhic decisor in the Monastir community before he was even thirty years old [cite: 3, 7].
Already in this early period his rock-like personality and his uncompromising stand on the standard of justice stood out [cite: 3]. His service in Monastir was cut short prematurely following a sharp confrontation that broke out between him and the rabbi of the local community [cite: 3]. The Maharival protested vigorously against acts of extortion and social injustice directed at members of the community, and when he saw that he could not eradicate the injustice from close at hand, he chose to leave his native city in the year 5294 (1534) and to emigrate to Salonika [cite: 3, 7].
The Salonika Years: Torah Leadership, Polemics and Personal Tragedy
The arrival of the Maharival in Salonika in the year 5294 (1534), when he was only about thirty, made a tremendous impression among the sages of the city [cite: 3, 4]. Evidence of his lofty standing within a short time is found in a public proclamation that was published in Salonika in that same year, which the Maharival signed in third place, immediately after the luminaries of the generation who were far older than he, Rabbi Yosef Taitazak and Rabbi Yosef Karo [cite: 3, 8]. In Salonika the Maharival was appointed av beit din (head of the rabbinic court) and head of a central yeshiva, and he raised many students [cite: 3].
His period in Salonika was characterized by vigorous public activity, but also by sharp polemics [cite: 3, 7]. As a judge and av beit din he fought resolutely against the wealthy of the community and its leaders who sought to exploit their standing in order to impose their will on the public [cite: 3, 7]. The beginning of the halakhic tension arose because of a deep Talmudic debate with Rabbi Shlomo Hasson [cite: 3, 7]. The Maharival exerted himself to resolve a severe difficulty raised by Rabbi Yitzchak of Corbeil (one of the Tosafists), while Rabbi Hasson claimed that it was no difficulty at all and objected to the words of the Tosafot [cite: 3]. The Maharival, who saw in this objection an improper disdain for the authority of the Rishonim, reacted very sharply, and the debate degenerated into a prolonged confrontation between the camps [cite: 3].
The polemic reached its peak in a head-on confrontation with Baruch, a wealthy and forceful communal leader (a former Converso from Portugal) who conducted himself with authority and a heavy hand [cite: 3, 7, 8]. The Maharival came out openly against his actions and was not deterred by his threats [cite: 3, 7, 8]. In the summer of the year 5305 (1545), the two met in the streets of Salonika, and Baruch had the audacity to slap the Maharival on his cheek in the sight of the entire public [cite: 3, 8]. The Maharival was shaken by the magnitude of this desecration of the honor of the Torah and raised a cry to heaven [cite: 3]. According to what is described in the sources of the period, that very night a huge fire broke out in Salonika that consumed about 5,000 houses and 18 synagogues, and claimed the lives of about 200 people [cite: 3, 8]. After the fire a severe plague spread through the city that felled hundreds more victims [cite: 3, 8].
During the days of the plague a mortal blow fell upon the Maharival: his firstborn son, Rabbi David, an eminent Torah scholar aged 28 who had fled to a nearby village from the plague, was murdered by assassins, allegedly at the behest of Baruch [cite: 3, 7]. Shortly afterwards, his second son, Moshe, drowned in a river while immersing [cite: 3, 7]. The double disaster and the heavy bereavement, together with the unceasing persecutions, cracked his frame and led him to the decision to leave Salonika [cite: 3, 7].
The Move to Constantinople, the Patronage of the Nasi Family and His Last Years
Around the year 5311 (1550) the Maharival moved his residence to the capital city, Constantinople [cite: 3, 7]. In Constantinople he found both spiritual and material refuge under the patronage of the valiant and generous woman known as Doña Gracia Mendes-Nasi and her son-in-law Don Joseph Nasi [cite: 3, 7, 8, 9]. Doña Gracia established an exalted yeshiva for him, supported his students, and provided him with the resources necessary so that he could devote himself entirely to disseminating Torah and to writing his halakhic responsa [cite: 3, 7, 8, 9].
In the year 5316 (1556) the Maharival fell ill with a severe and debilitating disease [cite: 3, 7]. From that time on, as a result of the suffering and afflictions that passed over him, he began to add to his signature in his responsa the painful title "the bitter and sighing" [cite: 3, 8]. He traveled for a certain period to Salonika in order to receive medical treatment and to print the first part of his book of responsa, and in his last years his eyes grew dim and he lost the light of his sight [cite: 3, 8, 9]. Despite his physical weakness, he continued to answer questions that reached him from all the Jewish communities [cite: 1, 3, 8]. The exact date of his death does not appear in the records, but the last mentions of his life are dated to the year 5339 (1578), and he departed to his eternal home in Constantinople around the year 5340 (1580), at about 75 years of age [cite: 3, 7, 8, 10].

His Public and Political Activity: The Polemic over the Ancona Boycott
The public involvement of the Maharival was not confined to the walls of the beit midrash alone, but encompassed geopolitical events with international implications for the Jewish people [cite: 2, 7]. The central event that displayed his resolute leadership was the polemic over the Ancona boycott, which took place between the years 5314 and 5316 (1554–1556) [cite: 3, 7].
The background to this grave polemic lay in the decrees of Pope Paul IV, who ordered the arrest of all the Conversos from Portugal who had settled in the port city of Ancona (which was under the rule of the Papal State), and had 24 of their brethren who remained loyal to their Judaism burned at the stake [cite: 3, 7]. In response to the cruel act, Doña Gracia Mendes-Nasi, together with her son-in-law Don Joseph Nasi, initiated a comprehensive commercial boycott of the port of Ancona [cite: 7]. The aim of the boycott was to transfer all the ship traffic and trade of the Jewish merchants in the Ottoman Empire from the port of Ancona to the nearby port of Pesaro (which was under the rule of the Duke of Urbino, who promised to protect the Conversos), and thereby to deal a mortal economic blow to the Papal State [cite: 7].
The proposed boycott aroused a harsh and stormy dispute among the rabbis of Constantinople and Salonika [cite: 7]. Opposing the position of the Nasi family stood the sage Rabbi Yehoshua Soncino, who feared that the boycott would cause the Pope to take revenge on the local Jews who remained in Ancona and to destroy the community entirely [cite: 7]. In contrast to him, the Maharival took his stand at the head of the supporters of the boycott and published a firm and reasoned halakhic responsum [cite: 3, 7]. In his ruling the Maharival determined that the community and its sages have full halakhic authority to impose ordinances and sanctions, and to compel all the merchants to comply with the boycott [cite: 3, 7]. His position was based on the concept of mutual responsibility, the duty of economic warfare against religious persecution, and the need to display Jewish strength in the face of the religious decrees in Europe [cite: 7].
Alongside the Ancona polemic, the Maharival stood at the forefront of the struggle against phenomena of informing and denunciation [cite: 3]. He signed severe bans against informers who endangered the welfare of the community, and even backed drastic measures against those who tried to harm the diplomatic activity of Don Joseph Nasi at the court of the Sultan [cite: 3].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Teachers, His Colleagues, His Beit Midrash and His Students
The tradition of learning of the Maharival rested on a glorious chain of transmission, but at the same time it raised a new generation of spiritual leaders who disseminated his Torah throughout the Jewish world [cite: 3, 4].
The Maharival received the foundations of his learning from his foremost teacher, Rabbi Yitzchak ibn Tzaddik ibn Lev, who imparted to him the fundamental Sephardic method of analysis [cite: 3, 4]. In the course of his career he maintained Torah ties and extensive halakhic correspondence with the great figures of the generation, among them Maran Rabbi Yosef Karo, Rabbi Yosef Taitazak, and the Maharashdam (Rabbi Shmuel de Medina) [cite: 3, 4, 5, 6]. Although he sometimes disagreed with them firmly on theoretical and halakhic issues, these sages held him in tremendous esteem and saw in him one of the pillars of the generation [cite: 3, 4, 5, 6, 11].
The beit midrash that Doña Gracia established for him in Constantinople became a Torah center to which outstanding students flocked, who took up central positions of leadership in the 16th and 17th centuries [cite: 3, 7, 9].

His Torah Works and the Literature of His Responsa
The written Torah legacy of the Maharival is concentrated mainly in his Book of Questions and Answers, alongside his theoretical novellae on the tractates of the Babylonian Talmud [cite: 3, 7, 9].
Responsa of the Maharival: Structure, Patterns and Style
The Book of Questions and Answers of the Maharival comprises four parts, which were printed in separate editions and in different places [cite: 3, 9]:
The first part of the book was first printed in the lifetime of the author, around the year 5318 (1558), at the printing house of Yosef Ya'avetz in Salonika (or in Constantinople) [cite: 9]. At the opening of the first part a short introduction by the author was printed, in which he expressly expresses gratitude to Doña Gracia Nasi and Don Joseph Nasi for the financial support that made possible the maintenance of his yeshiva [cite: 9]. On the first page, in place of a title page, the printer noted that following the burning of the Talmud in Italy in those days, he hoped that the printing of the responsa of the Maharival would pave the way for the printing of the entire Shas [cite: 9]. In addition, a famous and fundamental tract dealing with the laws of migo was appended to this part [cite: 9].
The second and third parts of the responsa were printed in Constantinople between the years 5321 and 5333 (1561–1573) [cite: 3]. The fourth part was printed after his death in the city of Kuru Çeşme (near Constantinople) in the year 5358 (1598) by his students [cite: 3]. A unique feature of the book of responsa is the incorporation of the glosses and novellae of his late son, Rabbi David [cite: 3, 7]. Out of a desire to commemorate his son who was murdered in the prime of his life, the Maharival wove David's comments into the body of the halakhic discussions, and sometimes even expanded upon them himself [cite: 3, 7]. As a result, some of the printers and scholars of later generations mistakenly attributed the son's novellae to the Maharival himself [cite: 3, 7].
Halakhic Novellae on the Shas
Alongside the practical issues presented in the responsa, the Maharival composed deep novellae on a number of central tractates of the Shas [cite: 3, 12, 13]. His work Chiddushei HaMaharival on tractate Gittin (and also on tractates Shevuot and Bava Kamma) is considered a theoretical masterpiece [cite: 3, 12, 14]. These novellae are characterized by a meticulous analysis of the language of the Gemara, Rashi and the Tosafot, and they received numerous mentions in the later exegetical literature [cite: 3, 12].

His Halakhic Method, His Method of Study and His Rulings
The Methodology of Study and the Demand for Theoretical Depth
The Maharival's method of study represents the peak of Talmudic analysis of the camp of the Sephardic sages in the Ottoman Empire [cite: 3, 7, 8]. In his halakhic responsa he does not content himself with presenting a fragmentary law or quoting authorities ready-made, but builds his answer starting from the fundamental Talmudic passage, proceeds to an analysis of the views of the Rishonim (the Rif, the Rambam, the Rosh, the Ritva and the Tosafot), and only afterwards draws the conclusion for practical halakha [cite: 3, 7, 15, 16].
His scholarly sharpness was renowned, and his responsa are characterized by a most intricate and profound structure, so much so that the sages of the generation noted that only outstanding Torah scholars are capable of descending to the depth of analysis of his responsa [cite: 3, 7, 8]. He used to test every line of reasoning with the talons of legitimate analysis and was not deterred from raising severe difficulties on the words of the great respondents who preceded him [cite: 3, 7].
His Foundational Ruling on the Status of the Conversos
One of the most significant halakhic contributions of the Maharival concerns the laws of marriage and lineage of the Conversos of Spain and Portugal [cite: 3, 17]. With the arrival of thousands of Conversos in the territories of the Ottoman Empire, difficult questions arose regarding women who had married as Conversas in the Iberian Peninsula, had fled alone, and wished to remarry in Israel [cite: 3, 17, 18].
The Maharival ruled as practical halakha that the betrothals of the Conversos that took place in Spain and Portugal are not valid betrothals at all by Torah law [cite: 3]. His reasoning was based on the halakhic understanding that these betrothals were performed in secrecy, in the absence of proper witnesses as required by law, and under circumstances in which full halakhic credibility did not apply to the acts of betrothal [cite: 3, 17, 18]. Since this was so, he determined that a woman who was betrothed as a Conversa in these places does not require a get from her first husband in order to remarry, and thereby he solved the grave problem of agunot that threatened to break apart many families in the community [cite: 3].
His Attitude to the Book "Beit Yosef": From an Initial Ban to Recognition of Divine Assistance
The story of the intellectual relationship between the Maharival and the monumental work of Maran Rabbi Yosef Karo, the book Beit Yosef, constitutes a fascinating chapter in the history of halakhic literature [cite: 7, 12, 19]:
Originally, the Maharival planned to compose by himself a comprehensive book that would gather all the sources and the views of the halakhic authorities around the four Turim [cite: 7]. When the book of Rabbi Yosef Karo was published in the year 5311 (1551), the Maharival feared sharply the pedagogical consequences of the work [cite: 7, 12]. He was concerned that the existence of a book that centralizes all the sources in a structured manner would lead to a decline in theoretical tension, and would cause the students to disdain direct toil in the passages of the Gemara and the words of the Rishonim [cite: 7, 12]. Therefore, he decreed a severe prohibition against bringing the book "Beit Yosef" within the walls of his yeshiva [cite: 7, 12].
The turning point occurred following a famous learning incident recorded in the literature of the generations [cite: 7, 12, 19]. While the Maharival was studying a difficult passage in the book of the Tur with his students, the Talmudic source of one of the laws eluded him [cite: 7, 12, 19]. After he had labored for a long time searching for the source and did not find it, he turned to his students and said that he saw that Heaven wants the book "Beit Yosef" to spread throughout the world [cite: 7, 12, 19]. He asked that the book be brought, and when they opened it they immediately found the elusive source explained in the words of the passage [cite: 7, 12, 19]. The Maharival immediately acknowledged that the merit and humility of Rabbi Yosef Karo had stood him in good stead from Heaven, canceled his decree, and permitted the study of the book to all his students [cite: 7, 12, 19].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Influence and Legacy for the Generations
The Tradition of "the Three Yosefs" and His Standing among the Halakhic Authorities
The Chida (Rabbi Chaim Yosef David Azulai), in his book Shem HaGedolim, cites an ancient and important tradition that defines the standing of the Maharival in the transitional generation [cite: 6, 9, 12, 19]:
"Know that I received from a man great in wisdom and fear of God, who received from a great rabbi, who received from the elders... that at the time of the destruction of the Talmud in Italy there was revealed badol of Maran, of blessed memory... who were fit, according to the generation, to write the comprehensive work, and in that generation there were three rabbis fit for this, and they are: the Rav Mohar"r Yosef Taitzak, and the Rav Maran [Rabbi Yosef Karo], and the Rav Maharival. And each one of them was fit for this task, and it was agreed from Heaven and the law was given by the holy Maran because of his exceeding humility" [cite: 5, 6, 9, 12, 19, 20].
This tradition places the Maharival as one of the only three greats of the generation who were capable, in terms of the scope of their wisdom and the depth of their analysis, of gathering the Torah of Israel and formulating the halakhic code of the Jewish people [cite: 5, 6, 9, 12, 19, 20].
Another exalted appraisal is cited in the name of the Gaon Rabbi Yitzchak Alfandari in the book "Magid Mereshit," which gathers the standing of the sages of the period [cite: 9, 11, 21]:
"The Maharival, the Maharashdam and the Maharashach – for us, are like the Rif, the Rambam and the Rosh in their time" [cite: 9, 11, 21].
This determination places the responsa and rulings of the Maharival in the position of a primary and absolute pillar of instruction for later generations, similar to the standing of the three pillars of instruction in the period of the Rishonim [cite: 9, 11, 21].
His Reception in the Literature of Halakha and Exegesis in the East and in Ashkenaz
The influence of the Maharival spread rapidly beyond the borders of the Ottoman Empire, and left an indelible mark on Talmudic study and halakhic ruling in all the Jewish communities [cite: 1, 2, 12, 20]:
In the literature of commentaries on the Shas, his work on tractate Gittin became one of the central sources discussed by the sages of Ashkenaz and Poland [cite: 12, 20]. The Maharsha (Rabbi Shmuel Eliezer HaLevi Eidels), in his novellae on tractate Gittin, cites the difficulties and answers of the Maharival frequently, referring to them with great respect and with the appellation "the Rav ben Lev asked" [cite: 12].
In the literature of halakhic ruling, the responsa of the Maharival serve as a fundamental decisive authority in the laws of monetary matters (Choshen Mishpat) and in the laws of marriage (Even HaEzer) [cite: 22, 23, 24, 25]. The great Ashkenazi halakhic authorities, such as the Maharshal (Rabbi Shlomo Luria), the Bach (Rabbi Yoel Sirkis), the Shach, and the Pitchei Teshuvah, cite the rulings of the Maharival as a fixed asset in halakhic ruling [cite: 20, 22, 23, 24, 25]. At the same time, the sages of Sepharad and the East – among them the Radbaz, the Mabit, his son the Maharit, and afterwards the Chida, the Chazon Ish, and Maran Rabbi Ovadia Yosef – saw in what is ruled in the responsa of the Maharival a first-rate source of ruling upon which the foundations of instruction rest [cite: 5, 8, 26, 27].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary and Conclusions
The figure of Rabbi Yosef ben David ibn Lev (the Maharival) stands in the annals of the Torah of Israel as one of the brilliant giants of the transitional generation from the Rishonim to the Acharonim [cite: 1, 3, 4]. The stormy course of his life – from his childhood in Monastir, through his public struggles and personal tragedies in Salonika, to the exalted dissemination of Torah under the patronage of Doña Gracia in Constantinople – attests to an eminent personality who paid a heavy personal price for uncompromising loyalty to the principles of Hebrew morality and law [cite: 3, 7, 8, 9].
His Torah thought, reflected in the four parts of the responsa of the Maharival and in his novellae on the tractates of the Shas, represents the peak of theoretical scholarship and resolute halakhic ruling [cite: 3, 7, 9, 12]. His halakhic determinations on the issue of the status of the Conversos, his leadership of the Ancona boycott, and his recognition of the heavenly superiority of the book "Beit Yosef," attest to the breadth of his horizons and his worthy leadership [cite: 3, 7, 12]. His legacy, which was established in the tradition of "the Three Yosefs" and was compared to the standing of the great Rishonim, continues to live and to influence the world of Torah, halakhic ruling and Talmudic analysis to this very day [cite: 6, 9, 11, 12].
